questions.q: What happens to the audit and approval stages when a rejected expense report is edited and resubmitted?
options: They are both skipped automatically on resubmission
Only approval restarts; audit is never run again
They restart from the beginning, since a resubmitted report isn't assumed fine just because it was reviewed once
The report is permanently blocked from resubmission
questions.explain: Resubmission restarts both the audit and approval stages from the beginning rather than resuming partway through.

questions.q: How does 'request more information' differ from a full rejection?
options: They are functionally identical in every way
Request more information always results in permanent denial
Request more information skips audit entirely
Request more information pauses the report for a specific clarification and resumes without restarting the whole sequence, unlike a full rejection
questions.explain: A request for more information is a lighter-touch pause that resumes at the same point once answered, rather than reopening the report for full edits and restarting the cycle.

questions.q: What is the correct way to fix an expense report that has already been accounted but not yet paid?
options: Put the specific invoice on hold in Payables and work the correction through Expenses before releasing it
Directly edit the posted accounting entry
Ignore the error since the report is already accounted
Delete the invoice from the General Ledger
questions.explain: Standard practice is to place the invoice on hold rather than letting an incorrect payment go out, then work the correction before releasing it.

questions.q: How is an expense report correction handled after the report has already been paid?
options: Through a reversing entry via Subledger Accounting, with a corrected item run through its own process, never a direct edit
By quietly overwriting the original journal entry
By asking the bank to cancel the payment with no accounting record
It cannot be corrected under any circumstances
questions.explain: Once paid, a posted transaction is never simply edited — it is reversed and replaced, preserving a clear audit trail.

questions.q: In the duplicate-hotel-item example, how was the accidental overpayment recovered?
options: It was written off with no further action
By deducting the duplicate amount from the employee's next approved expense report, with a documented note
By firing the employee
By reversing the employee's salary for the month
questions.explain: The overpayment was recovered as a deduction against the employee's next approved report, tracked clearly rather than silently erased.
